title: MCP 2026: Stateless Protocol, Enterprise Auth, and the July Release Candidate
content:
## Overview

Through 2026, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) steering group has been executing on a public roadmap aimed at making MCP production-ready at enterprise scale. The centerpiece is the **2026-07-28 release candidate**, described by the MCP team as the largest revision to the protocol since its November 2024 launch.

---

## Stateless Core

The headline architectural change is that MCP is now **stateless at the protocol layer**. Previously, MCP servers needed to manage sticky sessions and shared session state across requests, which complicated horizontal scaling. Under the 2026-07-28 RC:

- Servers can be load-balanced with a plain round-robin balancer
- No sticky sessions or shared session stores are required
- The protocol runs on ordinary HTTP infrastructure without special affinity routing

This directly addresses one of the most common complaints from teams running MCP servers behind standard cloud load balancers, where session-affinity requirements forced non-standard infrastructure.

---

## New Extensions

### MCP Apps
An extension for **server-rendered UI**. Instead of a tool returning only text or JSON, an MCP server can now render interactive UI that displays inside the host application (e.g., Claude Code, Claude.ai). This is distinct from Claude.ai's own Artifacts feature — MCP Apps UI is served by the MCP server itself, not generated by the model.

### Tasks Extension
Formalizes **long-running work** as a first-class protocol concept. Instead of a tool call blocking until completion (or the client polling ad hoc), a server can hand back a task handle that the client checks or subscribes to, letting operations that take minutes or hours (a large data export, a batch job) fit cleanly into the request/response model.

---

## Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA)

The EMA extension reached **stable** status in mid-2026 and aligns MCP's authorization flow more closely with existing enterprise identity standards — OAuth 2.1 and OpenID Connect — rather than a bespoke MCP-specific auth scheme. It has been adopted by Anthropic, Microsoft, and Okta, along with a growing number of third-party MCP servers. For organizations already running centralized identity providers, EMA lets MCP server access be governed by existing IdP policies instead of per-server credential management.

---

## Governance: A Formal Deprecation Policy

The 2026 roadmap also introduces a **formal deprecation policy** for the protocol itself — a defined process and timeline for retiring older protocol versions and extension APIs, giving server and client implementers a predictable upgrade path rather than ad hoc breaking changes.

---

## Why This Matters for Claude Code Users

Claude Code is one of the primary MCP clients in production use. The stateless core and EMA support mean MCP servers connected to Claude Code sessions (GitHub, Slack, Google Drive, and hundreds of community servers) can be deployed with standard cloud infrastructure and governed through existing enterprise SSO — removing two of the biggest operational blockers to running MCP servers at company scale.

Separately, Claude Code's own July 2026 update added the ability for **published Artifacts to call MCP connectors live** — each time someone views a shared artifact, it can call the viewer's own connected MCP tools to pull fresh data, rather than showing a static snapshot from when it was built. See the Claude Code Overview page for details.

---

## Adoption Signal

The AI Agent Infrastructure Foundation (AAIF) held the MCP Dev Summit North America in New York City in April 2026, drawing roughly 1,200 attendees — an indicator of how far MCP adoption has grown since its 2024 introduction as an Anthropic-authored open standard.
